headline: Oura sued for allegedly misleading consumers about sleep-tracking accuracy
summary: A class action lawsuit claims Oura rings use AI-generated estimates with a 'coin flip's chance' of being correct, despite marketing them as highly accurate.
details: A proposed class action lawsuit accuses smart ring maker Oura of deceiving consumers about the accuracy of its sleep tracking features. The suit alleges Oura rings are unable to measure the physiological signals needed to assess sleep quality or determine sleep stages.

Instead, the lawsuit claims Oura relies on AI-generated estimates that have a "coin flip's chance of being correct." This follows years of user complaints about the smart ring's sleep accuracy, with some reporting their devices indicated optimal sleep despite users feeling unwell.

The complaint states Oura marketed its rings, priced at $300 and up, as "built for accuracy" and offering "unparalleled accuracy," even claiming 95% sleep-staging accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs.

The lawsuit argues Oura cannot measure sleep or cycles because "sleep happens in the brain, not on one's finger." It seeks to stop Oura from misrepresenting its products and requests restitution for affected consumers.

Ryan Clarkson, co-founder of Clarkson Law Firm, stated, "When people rely on a device to guide decisions about their health, misinformation cannot be tolerated." He emphasized that people alter their lives based on these figures.
caption:
Oura rings are allegedly misleading consumers about sleep-tracking accuracy, according to a new class action lawsuit.

A proposed class action lawsuit accuses smart ring maker Oura of deceiving consumers about the accuracy of its sleep tracking features. The suit alleges Oura rings are unable to measure the physiological signals needed to assess sleep quality or determine sleep stages.

Instead, the lawsuit claims Oura relies on AI-generated estimates that have a "coin flip's chance of being correct." This follows years of user complaints about the smart ring's sleep accuracy, with some reporting their devices indicated optimal sleep despite users feeling unwell.

The complaint states Oura marketed its rings, priced at $300 and up, as "built for accuracy" and offering "unparalleled accuracy," even claiming 95% sleep-staging accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs.

The lawsuit argues Oura cannot measure sleep or cycles because "sleep happens in the brain, not on one's finger." It seeks to stop Oura from misrepresenting its products and requests restitution for affected consumers.

Ryan Clarkson, co-founder of Clarkson Law Firm, stated, "When people rely on a device to guide decisions about their health, misinformation cannot be tolerated." He emphasized that people alter their lives based on these figures.
